title: "Coaching your QA and reporting upward"
order: 38

## The ticket

Three documents, three months, one desk: the ICCBBA (International Council for Commonality in
Blood Banking Automation) deviation and CAPA (corrective and preventive action) packet, the OS
patch's validation impact assessment, and the BECS (Blood Establishment Computer Software)
vendor reassessment. Different systems, different regulatory hooks, same Quality Analyst (QA).
And now that you've reviewed all three, you can't unsee the shape underneath them.

Every one of her conclusions was defensible on the merits. "Not reportable" was very likely
right. "No impact to the validated state" was very likely right. "Continue using the vendor"
was very likely right. And every single time, the reasoning that would have proven it was
missing from the page — and every single time, she'd stopped at the first source that sounded
credible instead of the one that actually settled the question: a supervisor's word instead of
a BECS query, a vendor's release notes instead of Lakeshore's own test, a vendor's "yes" instead
of the deviation record sitting one click away that said the opposite.

That's not three unrelated documents with three unrelated problems. That's one QA with one
coachable pattern, showing up three times because nobody's named it to her as a pattern yet.

Then, Thursday, her first draft of next quarter's management-review packet lands in your inbox.
You already know what a superficial one looks like — `quality-system-essentials` showed you,
months ago, in a lesson you weren't the one drafting: *"Internal audit: 4 sites reviewed, 1
finding, corrective action initiated. CAPA log: 5 closed this quarter, 3 open. Change control:
12 changes processed, no overdue verifications. Risk management: FMEA on file for the
distribution process."* Her draft reads almost identically. Every line true. Every line, on its
own, close to useless — no trend, no aging, no sense of whether anything is getting better or
worse, nothing a room full of executives could actually decide something from.

Two problems, one root: your QA is good, and she's stopped short twice — once in how she writes
a conclusion, once in how she reports a system. Both are fixable. Neither gets fixed by you
doing it for her.

## Why this matters — and the ITIL bridge

You already know how to grow a direct report past a recurring gap in their work, because you've
done it in code review. A junior engineer whose pull requests keep the same shape — logic that's
usually right, but undocumented edge cases, or a habit of trusting the first Stack Overflow
answer instead of reading the actual library docs — doesn't improve because you rewrite their
diffs for them every time. They improve because you keep asking the same question until asking
it becomes their own habit: "what happens if this input is null?" Rewriting the code ships that
one PR faster. It also guarantees you'll be asking the same question next sprint, because the
engineer never had to build the muscle themselves.

That's the strongest bridge in this module, and it runs in both directions. **The reward for an
engineer whose changes keep passing review clean isn't more scrutiny — it's a standard change:
pre-approved, no CAB (change advisory board) review required, because their track record has
earned it.** Widening your QA's decision rights as her judgment proves out is the exact same
mechanism, wearing quality-system clothes instead of change-management ones. Trust earned on the
page gets spent as autonomy off it.

Two more bridges, both for the second half of this module — reporting upward. You've certainly
seen a **"watermelon" SLA (service-level agreement) report**: green on every summary tile, red
the moment you open the ticket underneath it. A quality-metrics packet can do the exact same
thing: "5 CAPAs closed, 3 open" looks green. It says nothing about whether those three open CAPAs
are two weeks old or eleven months old, or whether the five closed ones closed on a passed
effectiveness check or just on "the fix shipped." Same watermelon, different fruit stand.

And you know **CSI (continual service improvement)** — the ITIL practice of defining CSFs
(critical success factors) and the KPIs (key performance indicators) that measure them at the
*service* level, deliberately separate from any one engineer's personal metrics, because
conflating the two breaks both. A CSF like "incidents resolved within SLA" measures the system.
An engineer's personal ticket count measures a person, and the moment the system metric becomes
the person's target, people start closing tickets to hit the number instead of fixing things.
That's exactly where this module's KPI design lands.

## The rule in plain English

Two threads, and they share one root cause: a genuinely good QA who hasn't yet been taught,
explicitly, that "usually right" isn't the bar, and that a count isn't a report.

### Thread one: coaching the pattern

**Name the pattern once, not three separate times.** You've caught, individually, in
`reviewing-deviations-and-capas`, `reviewing-validation-packages`, and
`reviewing-vendor-risk-assessments`: (1) **right conclusion, reasoning off the page** — her
calls hold up, but the path to them doesn't survive on paper; and (2) **stops at the first
credible source** — a supervisor's statement, a vendor's release notes, a vendor's own
questionnaire answer, each accepted as proof instead of as a lead. Naming this once, as one
pattern with two parts, does something three separate corrections never will: it tells her what
to watch for in her *own* next document, before you ever see it, instead of teaching her "fix
this specific line" three times in a row with no throughline between them.

**Questions, not rewrites.** The single most important mechanical choice in this module. If you
rewrite her reportability paragraph, her test-scope conclusion, or her risk-tier reasoning
yourself, you've fixed that document and trained her to wait for your red pen on the next one.
Every review module in this course already modeled the alternative: "What BECS record shows none
of the 40 units shipped?" not "Add the distribution query." A question makes her do the thinking
that produces judgment. A rewrite makes you do it, permanently, for as long as she works for you.

**Her self-check.** The payoff of teaching her the cold-read test by name, instead of just using
it on her work silently, is that it can become *her* instrument before it's ever yours again.
Ask her, directly, to run Conclusion, Evidence, Reasoning, Criteria first, Decision trail, and
Loose ends on her own draft before it reaches your desk — same six questions, same order, every
time. A QA who catches her own "stops at the first source" gap before she routes the document
has caught it the way an assessor would, which is the finish line this course has been building
toward.

**The delegation ladder.** Three positions, and movement between them is earned or lost on
evidence, never on a hunch:

1. **"I review everything."** Where you start with any document type she's new to, or any
   document type where you've seen the pattern recently and haven't yet seen it corrected.
2. **"I sample."** You spot-check a subset — say, every third document, or anything above a
   defined risk threshold — instead of reading every line of everything. This is where a QA
   moves once she's shown, across several real documents, that she catches her own gaps before
   you do.
3. **"You decide, I'm informed."** Reserved for the routine, well-precedented calls
   `qa-deliverables-and-ownership` already named as hers alone — closing a low-severity
   deviation with a documented cause and no CAPA, a minor document revision. You're on the
   notification list, not the approval chain.

**Widen on evidence, narrow on a miss — without drama.** The ladder moves up when she's
demonstrated the judgment, in writing, more than once: a reportability call with the reasoning
on the page, a "no impact" conclusion backed by Lakeshore's own check instead of a vendor's word.
It moves back down when a real miss gets through — not as punishment, but as a plain, unemotional
fact: "this is why I'm back to reading these closely for a while; show me a few more clean ones
and we'll widen it again." A ladder that only ever moves in one direction isn't measuring
judgment, it's measuring seniority. One that narrows *punitively* — in a way that makes the next
miss less likely to get reported honestly — defeats its own purpose, the trap this module names
below.

**Documented competence, not just your impression of her.** AABB's Quality System Essentials
framework — paraphrased, no standard number, from `sources/aabb/qse-framework.md` — places
competence assessment and training under **Resources** (QSE 2): a blood establishment is
expected to track staff competence formally, as records, not as a manager's private sense that
someone's gotten better. Her growth on exactly this pattern — reasoning shown on the page,
sourcing that goes past the first credible answer — belongs in her own competence record, tied
to real documents she produced. 21 CFR 606.20(b), already quoted in
`qa-deliverables-and-ownership`, sets the regulatory floor underneath this: personnel must have
"a thorough understanding of the procedures or control operations they perform." A widening
delegation ladder with nothing written down to justify it is exactly the kind of gap this course
has taught you to catch in *her* documents. Don't leave the same gap in yours.

**Coach the write-up. Never the quality outcome.** `qa-deliverables-and-ownership` drew this
line the first week: you own supervisory review — is the document defensible? — and never own
the quality decision itself. That line gets genuinely hard to hold here, and it's worth naming
the hard case directly instead of pretending it away. Say you're coaching her, repeatedly, on
"show your reasoning before you state a conclusion." At some point that coaching, followed
consistently, might mean she writes toward a conclusion you'd have preferred she reach faster —
and it can start to feel, to both of you, like coaching her writing is nudging her toward a
particular answer. It isn't, if you hold the line precisely: your feedback can demand that the
reasoning behind *whatever conclusion she reaches* is on the page. It can never suggest which
conclusion the reasoning should support. "Show me the evidence behind 'not reportable'" is
coaching the write-up. "I'd expect this one to land as reportable" is coaching the outcome, and
it's a line you don't cross even under real pressure — a tight deadline, a CIO (chief information
officer) asking why quality keeps blocking IT's schedule. The moment your feedback starts
sounding like a preference for which way a call goes, stop, and ask whether you're still
reviewing the document or quietly trying to write it.

### Thread two: reporting upward

**Rebuild the packet, by coaching her to build it — not by building it yourself.** Here's the
superficial version again, quoted exactly as `internal-audits-and-management-review` presented
it, because your QA's draft reads almost the same:

> *Internal audit: 4 sites reviewed, 1 finding, corrective action initiated.*
> *CAPA log: 5 closed this quarter, 3 open.*
> *Change control: 12 changes processed, no overdue verifications.*
> *Risk management: FMEA on file for the distribution process.*

Every line is a count. None of them is an analysis. Here's the same information, rebuilt with
the three things that turn a count into something a management review can actually act on —
**trend** (is this number rising, falling, or flat against recent quarters?), **aging** (how
old are the open items, against Lakeshore's own targets?), and **effectiveness-pass rate** (of
what's marked "closed," how much closed on real effectiveness data instead of just "the fix
shipped"?):

> *Internal audit: 4 sites reviewed this cycle, 1 finding — Fairview's binder gap, RPN 50.
> Finding rate: 1 per 4 sites this cycle, down from 2 per 4 last cycle. Corrective action
> initiated; extent-of-condition check of all satellite sites in progress, due [date].*
>
> *CAPA log: 8 total open across the quarter. 5 closed — 4 with a passed effectiveness check
> on file, 1 closed on implementation evidence only (flagged for reopening review). 3 still
> open, average age 40 days against Lakeshore's 60-day target; oldest is CAPA-1147-A at 55
> days, on track. Trending down from last quarter's average age of 65 days.*
>
> *Change control: 12 changes processed, verifications on time in 11 of 12 (92%); one
> verification 3 days late, root cause and corrective step noted. Compares to 10 of 11 (91%)
> last quarter — flat, watching for drift.*
>
> *Risk management: FMEA on file for the distribution process; one open validation impact
> assessment (VIA-0842) closed this cycle, with a decision-trail gap corrected before
> production sign-off. Vendor reassessment (VRA-0219) current as of this cycle; one contract
> follow-up still open, owner and date assigned.*

Notice what didn't change: every underlying fact is one this course already established. What
changed is that each line now answers "so what" instead of stopping at "here's a number." That's
the whole difference between a packet that looks complete and one that shows a system actually
working. **Your job in this thread is coaching her to produce this version herself** — asking
"what's the trend against last quarter?" and "which of those five closures had a passed
effectiveness check?" — not quietly rewriting her draft the night before the meeting. Same rule
as thread one, applied to a different document.

**System measures and her performance measures never share a line.** This is the single most
important design rule in this thread: **deviation count can never be her individual target.**
The moment "keep your open-deviation count low" becomes something her performance review looks
at, you've built an incentive to under-report — to call something a training note instead of a
deviation, to close early instead of thoroughly. A quality system that measures deviations to
find and fix problems, and simultaneously punishes the person who reports them, is working
against itself. This is Goodhart's-law territory: a measure that's useful for judging the
*system* stops being trustworthy the instant it becomes a *target* for the person whose job is to
report into it honestly.

Two separate lists follow from that rule, and they should never blend into one shared
scorecard:

**Candidate system measures** — about the quality system as a whole, reported upward, never
assigned to her as a personal number to hit:

- Deviation cycle time (discovery to disposition)
- CAPA aging and on-time rate against Lakeshore's own targets
- Effectiveness-check first-pass rate — of CAPAs claiming closure, how many passed their
  effectiveness check the first time, without extension or reopening
- Repeat-root-cause rate — how often the same underlying cause resurfaces across separate
  events, the clearest possible signal that a "fix" didn't actually fix the system
- Change verifications completed on time
- Validation impact assessments completed and approved before deployment, not after
- Vendor reassessments current against their own review schedule

**Her own performance measures** — about her work, distinct from the system's health:

- Rework rate on her submissions — how often a document she routes to you needs a "must fix
  before I sign" round versus going through clean
- On-time delivery against agreed review and reassessment schedules
- Trend in review findings per document, over time — fewer must-fix findings per document,
  quarter over quarter, is real, visible evidence of the coaching in thread one working

Read those two lists side by side and notice what they don't share: nothing about *how many*
deviations, CAPAs, or findings exist appears on her list. Volume belongs to the system. Quality
of write-up and reliability of delivery belong to her.

**Leading versus lagging.** A lagging indicator tells you what already happened — a deviation
count, last quarter's CAPA closures. A leading indicator tells you what's likely to happen next,
early enough to still change it — CAPA aging trending up before it breaches its
effectiveness-check window, her rework rate climbing before a "must fix" gap reaches a document
that matters, a vendor reassessment slipping past its due date before the vendor relationship
causes a problem. A packet built entirely on lagging indicators is a rearview mirror. One that
tracks a couple of leading indicators alongside them is the only version that lets anyone in the
room actually prevent something, instead of just explaining it afterward.

**Your own report to the CIO.** Everything above feeds one more document: your own one-page
quarterly report, up to your CIO, merging quality, IT, and risk into something a non-specialist
executive can act on in five minutes. Keep it to the same discipline this whole course has
taught: one page, trend and aging over raw counts, and — critically — **one decision asked**,
not a status update with no ask attached. A strong candidate sits right in this quarter's own
numbers: `internal-audits-and-management-review` already named the still-unbuilt automated
document-control review-date trigger as something management review flagged needing funding.
That's a real, concrete decision with a dollar figure and an owner — "fund the review-date
trigger this quarter, or accept that satellite-site binder audits stay manual and keep finding
gaps like Fairview's" — not a vague request for "more quality resources." A report that ends
without a specific ask is the executive-level version of the same watermelon problem: it looks
like a briefing, and it produces nothing anyone can decide on.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 606.20(b) | "Six-oh-six point twenty, paragraph b" | Personnel performing regulated steps must be adequate in training and experience, with "a thorough understanding of the procedures or control operations they perform." Already quoted in full in `qa-deliverables-and-ownership`. | The regulatory floor under "documented competence" — reused, not re-fetched, as the baseline her growth records sit on top of. |

That's the whole table. This module is mostly synthesis of material this course and
`quality-system-essentials` already taught; it doesn't need a new citation to carry it.

## The actual text

606.20(b), quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.20.md`, reused from `qa-deliverables-and-ownership`:

> All personnel shall have capabilities commensurate with their assigned functions, a thorough
> understanding of the procedures or control operations they perform, the necessary training or
> experience, and adequate information concerning the application of pertinent provisions of
> this part to their respective functions.

Read it as a floor, not a coaching program: the regulation requires personnel to be competent
for what they do. It says nothing about *how* Lakeshore demonstrates that competence, tracks its
growth, or documents a delegation ladder widening as judgment improves — that structure is
AABB's, not FDA's.

AABB's Quality System Essentials framework, paraphrased only, no standard number, from
`sources/aabb/qse-framework.md`: **Resources** (QSE 2) covers job qualifications, competence
assessment, and training as an ongoing program with its own records — not a one-time hiring bar,
and not a manager's private impression. That's the structure this module's "documented
competence" point rests on. **Organization** (QSE 1), already named in
`internal-audits-and-management-review`, is what actually requires management review with
defined inputs — not any specific KPI, and not any specific formula. That's the exact hook
behind this module's regulatory-requirement question, below: which measures Lakeshore tracks,
and how it calculates them, is Lakeshore's own choice, built on top of a requirement to review
*something* meaningful, not a menu FDA or AABB hands you pre-filled.

## What an inspector or assessor would actually look for

**For coaching and delegation**, evidence that growth is real and recorded, not just felt. A
competence record showing specific documents reviewed, specific gaps found and corrected over
time, and a delegation level that changed on a dated basis tied to that evidence — not a
training certificate from three years ago and nothing since. An assessor watching a widening
ladder will also ask the harder question: what happens when a miss gets through anyway? A
documented, undramatic narrowing — not silence — reads as a functioning review structure. A
ladder that only ever widens reads as a program that isn't actually watching.

**For management review**, exactly what `internal-audits-and-management-review` already told
you to expect, now with your own fingerprints on it: minutes showing trend and aging analysis,
not raw counts, and documented decisions with owners and dates attached. An assessor reading
your packet next to last quarter's will check whether the numbers move in a direction that makes
sense given what was reported as "fixed" — a CAPA aging metric that never improves despite a
stream of "closed" CAPAs is itself a finding.

**For your own review discipline**, evidence you actually reviewed the packet before it went
upward. Questions on the draft, a dated mark distinguishing your read from a rubber stamp, and —
the tell an assessor or your own CIO notices fastest — a report that changes meaningfully quarter
to quarter instead of reading like the same four bullet points with new numbers dropped in.

## Common traps

**Rewriting instead of asking.** The most tempting shortcut in this module, especially under a
deadline: it's Thursday, the meeting is Friday, and it's faster to rewrite her packet's bullets
into trend-and-aging form yourself than to send it back and wait for a second draft. Do it once
and you've taught her a rushed first draft is fine, because you'll always catch it. Do it twice
and it stops being a review — it's you writing the packet with her name on the byline.

**Making deviation count her personal target.** The sharpest trap in this module: the instant a
system measure becomes her individual number, you've built an incentive to under-report, and you
won't find out until an assessor — or a real event — finds what she quietly didn't write up.

**Treating "watermelon" metrics as healthy because the summary line looks fine.** "5 CAPAs
closed, 3 open" is green on the outside. Whether it's red inside depends entirely on aging and
effectiveness-pass rate you can't see from the count alone.

**Narrowing delegation punitively.** Pulling back to "I review everything" the moment a miss
surfaces, with blame attached, teaches the safest move next time is not mentioning the miss at
all. Narrowing has to be plain, undramatic, and explicitly temporary — "here's why, and here's
what gets us back to sampling" — or it trains the same under-reporting instinct as the KPI trap,
aimed at your relationship instead of a metric.

## What this means for your job

- **Name the pattern once, out loud, across documents — not the same correction three separate
  times with no throughline.** "Right conclusion, reasoning off the page, and stops at the first
  credible source" is a sentence she can carry into her next document herself.
- **Ask questions on every review, every time, no matter how short on time you are.** Rewrite
  instead of ask and you've traded one better document for a QA who trusts your red pen more
  than her own judgment.
- **Ask her to run the cold-read test on her own draft before it reaches you, and check that she
  actually did.** Her self-check is the entire payoff of teaching her the instrument by name.
- **Move the delegation ladder on evidence, in writing, in both directions — never on a hunch,
  and never with drama.** A widening you can't point to a document for isn't delegation, it's
  assumption. A narrowing with blame teaches concealment.
- **Before you sign off on any KPI, ask whether it's measuring the system or measuring her.** If
  a metric would make her look worse for reporting a real problem honestly, it's the wrong
  metric.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: "FDA requires blood centers to track specific quality KPIs — deviation cycle time, CAPA aging, effectiveness-check pass rate." True or false?

False. This curriculum's sources show no FDA regulation naming a specific quality KPI, formula,
or dashboard metric for a blood establishment to track. What AABB's Organization QSE actually
requires (paraphrase, no standard number) is a management review, on a defined cadence, using
real inputs to produce real decisions — it doesn't specify which measures satisfy that, or how
to calculate them. Which KPIs Lakeshore tracks, and their exact formulas — deviation cycle time
in days, CAPA on-time rate as a percentage against a chosen target window — are Lakeshore's own
management choices, built to satisfy a real requirement to review the system meaningfully, not a
menu handed down by a regulator or a standard.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Your QA's third document in a row shows the same "stops at the first credible source" gap. You're behind on your own work this week. Fastest fix: rewrite the weak section yourself and send it back clean, or send it back with a question and wait for round two?

Send it back with a question, even though it's slower this week. A rewrite fixes this one
document and guarantees you'll be finding the same gap in her fourth, fifth, and sixth — because
she never had to build the judgment that catches it herself. A question — "what's the source
behind this claim, and does it actually cover the whole thing you're claiming?" — costs a day
now and is the only move that changes what her *next* document looks like before it ever reaches
your desk. The pattern only stops repeating once catching it is her habit, not yours.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Your QA proposes a new individual performance goal for herself: "Close 90% of deviations within 30 days of discovery." Reasonable KPI to approve?

No — not as an individual target, even though it sounds disciplined. Deviation-related counts
and timelines are system measures: useful for judging whether Lakeshore's quality system is
healthy, dangerous the moment they become a personal number she's evaluated against. A 30-day
personal closure target pressures her to close a deviation before the investigation is actually
done, or to avoid opening a borderline one at all, just to protect the number. The system-level
version — deviation cycle time, tracked as a trend — belongs in the management-review packet.
Her own performance measures should track her rework rate and on-time delivery, not the raw
count or speed of the events she's reporting on.
:::

## Where this goes next

This closes `directing-the-quality-analyst`. Across six modules, you learned to read four kinds
of document your QA produces — a deviation and CAPA packet, a validation impact assessment, a
vendor risk assessment, and a management-review packet — with one shared instrument, the
cold-read test; to sort what it finds with gap triage; to know which events have to reach you,
and how fast, before a document ever exists to review; and now, to coach the person writing all
of it, and to report what you're seeing upward in a way that shows trend and improvement instead
of just a list of things that went wrong.

Three places to go from here, each picking up something this course deliberately left alone.
`fda-and-aabb-in-practice`, not yet built, is where audit-program design lives — an actual audit
schedule, auditor independence and competency, evidence sampling — along with facing an FDA
inspection or AABB assessment directly. `csv-and-becs` and `vendor-and-third-party-risk-management`,
also not yet built, are where modules 4 and 5's decision-trail-only scope gets its full technical
depth: validation methodology, GAMP 5 (Good Automated Manufacturing Practice), and IQ/OQ/PQ for
the first; SOC 2 mechanics and vendor risk-tiering methodology for the second. And if what you
want next is the complete version of the bridge this module only sketched — translating quality
and IT metrics for an executive audience, and the full ITIL-to-QSE (Quality System Essential)
crosswalk — that's `itsm-for-regulated-blood-services`, the track built to own that translation
in full.
